{"id": "7:180/q32", "question": "What further inward insights are drawn from divine names?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:180/q32/p1", "position": "Names mediate creation, provision and transformation of the caller.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says created perfections point back to divine names and needs seek their sustaining attribute. Sufi dhikr cultivates virtues. The hidden-name report has three revealed names and one concealed; the Najmiyya account distinguishes eternal essential and created action names. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī interprets Allah, Tabāraka and Taʿālā as encompassing perfection, bestowal of blessing and transcendence from deficiency; a transmitted account even counts 'neither slumber nor sleep overtakes Him' as a broad descriptive name."}, {"id": "7:180/q32/p2", "position": "Spiritual helpers and truthful knowledge of the Messenger manifest divine nearness.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says God's people sustain truth, bring relief and rain, and that experiential knowers perceive the Prophet's nearness; his character and its effects witness against fabrication."}, {"id": "7:180/q32/p3", "position": "The Imams are called God's beautiful names as signs through whom servants know Him.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAbd Allāh reports that deeds are accepted through knowledge of the Imams; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī explains name broadly as verbal or nonverbal indicator and the prophets and successors as complete servants."}]}
{"id": "7:180/q33", "question": "How do related discussions of names illuminate Qurʾanic initials and Allāhumma?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:180/q33/p1", "position": "Some take disconnected opening letters as keys or fragments of divine names.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās connects alif, lām and mīm to Allah, Laṭīf and Majīd and glosses ALM, ALMS and ALR as divine declarations. Al-Rabīʿ adds favors, trials and lifespans; Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says an unknown arrangement would disclose the Greatest Name. Ibn Fāris praises this."}, {"id": "7:180/q33/p2", "position": "Others treat the letters as unknown secrets, sura titles, Qurʾan names, scribal signs or oaths.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī reports Abū Bakr, al-Shaʿbī and Ibn Fāris on hidden knowledge, and known-meaning, oath, revelation-marker and sura-title views. Bint al-Shāṭi says later interpreters mostly elaborate earlier views. Al-Zarkashī also explains letter-form spelling and vocative alif omission."}, {"id": "7:180/q33/p3", "position": "Qurʾanic sciences frame these issues through revelation, language, readings, exegesis, orthography and worship.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī and al-Zarkashī list places and occasions, textual variants, parsing, virtues, abrogation, coherence and devotion; these notes provide taxonomy rather than another reading of this verse."}, {"id": "7:180/q33/p4", "position": "Allāhumma is a vocative or a condensed invocation of all God's names.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī reports the usual replaced yā with doubled mīm, a compound etymology, Abū Rajāʾ's seventy names, Ibn Ẓafar's Greatest Name and ninety-nine attributes, and al-Ḥasan's and al-Naḍr's encompassing-prayer views."}]}
{"id": "7:180/q34", "question": "What related notes concern adjacent wording and prayer reports?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:180/q34/p1", "position": "Additional reports promise answered prayer by the names and cite a prayer for divine aid.", "reasons": "One report promises response to whoever calls by the ninety-nine; al-Qurṭubī cites a prophetic prayer for help, victory and favorable plotting, graded ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ."}, {"id": "7:180/q34/p2", "position": "Adjacent wording distinguishes pregnancy from carried loads and weight-bearing.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash distinguishes ḥaml from ḥiml, explains athqalat by analogy with becoming possessed of dates or milk, and reports a vocalized reading."}]}
{"id": "7:201/q01", "question": "Who are those who have taqwa here, and what do they avoid?", "turns_on": "Whether taqwa names general faith and obedience, only avoidance of shirk, protection from punishment, a special prophetic class, or an inward state.", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q01/p1", "position": "They are believers or righteous people generally, guarding against disobedience and fulfilling God's commands.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Ibn Abbas, al-Baghawi and al-Wahidi identify them as believers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nahhas include obedience and avoidance of sins; al-Tabrisi says avoiding disobedience; Ibn Atiyya insists praise here requires avoidance of both shirk and sins, not shirk alone. Alusi says the relative phrase is unrestricted. Bursevi defines taqwa as protection from harm. Ibn Ashur includes messengers and righteous followers as exemplars, citing 2:2."}, {"id": "7:201/q01/p2", "position": "They are people who avoid shirk, or shirk and grave indecencies.", "reasons": "Muqatil specifies avoidance of polytheism; al-Kalbi adds unbelief and grave indecencies; Qashani and Alusi give the shirk-only sense in their inward gloss."}, {"id": "7:201/q01/p3", "position": "They are those guarding against God's punishment.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports this third explanation without naming an authority."}, {"id": "7:201/q01/p4", "position": "They are resolute messengers if the preceding address is specific, or righteous servants if it is general.", "reasons": "An unnamed critical scholar makes the referent depend on the scope of 7:200. Alusi disputes the necessity of restricting it to messengers."}, {"id": "7:201/q01/p5", "position": "They are non-prophets in contrast to Muhammad in the preceding address.", "reasons": "Some say a mere initial nazgh affects the Prophet whereas an established mass affects other pious people, as a sign of prophetic favor."}, {"id": "7:201/q01/p6", "position": "They are people of the heart whose taqwa is a light that distinguishes truth and falsehood.", "reasons": "Al-Ta'wilat al-Najmiyya cites the Prophet's indication toward his chest as evidence that taqwa resides in the heart."}]}
{"id": "7:201/q02", "question": "What does 'touches them' convey?", "turns_on": "Whether mass emphasizes minimal contact or a stronger stage than nazgh in 7:200.", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q02/p1", "position": "Mass is literal contact by hand, used figuratively for affliction or even the slightest onset of temptation.", "reasons": "Jishumi and Ibn Ashur give the hand-contact sense; Jishumi notes water reached by hands and affliction by jinn, as does al-Tabrisi. Ibn Ashur stresses even slight contact and, with conditional idha, intervention before thought grows into resolve. Bursevi calls it the slightest prompting."}, {"id": "7:201/q02/p2", "position": "The touch is a stronger incursion than the preceding nazgh.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan contrasts bodily contact with the lighter movement nazgh; Razi similarly says a ṭāʾif touching the pious is more forceful than an initial nudge. Others distinguish established contact for non-prophets from initial prompting for Muhammad; another account says Satan makes greater effort against the perfect."}]}
{"id": "7:201/q03", "question": "How is ṭāʾif or ṭayf read?", "turns_on": "Transmission of the named readers and whether the forms are equivalent, distinct, or an original doubled form.", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q03/p1", "position": "Ṭāʾif, with alif and hamza.", "reasons": "Most Medinan and Kufan readers in al-Tabari; Nafi, Asim, Ibn Amir and Hamza in Ibn Mujahid and others; reported also from Jabir's hearing of the Prophet and from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Some reports assign both Basrans and Meccans to this reading. Al-Tabari prefers it because anger or lapse fits a circling whisper more closely than an apparition."}, {"id": "7:201/q03/p2", "position": "Ṭayf, without alif.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr and al-Kisai are repeatedly named; Baydawi, Alusi and Ibn Ashur add Yaqub. Reports also name al-Nakhai, al-Aswad, al-Amash, Ibn Yazid, al-Jahdari and Talha, and some locate it among Meccans and Basrans. The two readings are often called dialectal variants."}, {"id": "7:201/q03/p3", "position": "Ṭayyif, with doubled yāʾ and no alif.", "reasons": "Reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and also Ibn Abbas, al-Jahdari and al-Dahhak. Grammarians take it as evidence for an original doubled form, though al-Nahhas calls the undoubled ṭayf normal Arabic."}]}
{"id": "7:201/q04", "question": "What does ṭāʾif or ṭayf mean in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse names a general satanic incursion or a specific instance such as anger, a sin, fear or seizure.", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q04/p1", "position": "It is a passing satanic visitation or prompting, including whispering and temptation.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas calls it lamma, touch, whisper or incitement; Abu Amr calls it whispering. Al-Tabari generalizes anger and intrusion to any misguiding prompt. Al-Layth describes whispering enveloping a person; Taj al-Arus includes an elusive image or obsession, whence Asad's 'dark suggestion.' Study Quran links whispering to 114:4. Ibn Ashur likens it to a visitor circling for entry; Arab guests circled a house, and he cites al-Nabigha, the Kaaba and al-A'sha. Itqan records the Thaqif dialect sense 'sting.'"}, {"id": "7:201/q04/p2", "position": "It is anger.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Said and others repeatedly explain the touch this way. Al-Wahidi and Razi say anger resembles madness because reason deserts the angry person; some read the verse as anger accompanied by Satan's making wrongdoing attractive. Al-Tabari regards anger as one instance within the broader satanic prompting."}, {"id": "7:201/q04/p3", "position": "It is a sin or the temptation to commit one.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbi calls it sin; other reports place the pious either on the brink of an indecent act or after a lapse. Ibn Kathir lists intending and committing a sin among the reported explanations."}, {"id": "7:201/q04/p4", "position": "It is fear or alarm.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi transmits this gloss from Sa'id ibn Jubayr."}, {"id": "7:201/q04/

{"id": "7:201/q05", "question": "How do the forms ṭāʾif and ṭayf relate in sense and formation?", "turns_on": "Whether the two forms are synonymous, mark different kinds of visitation, or are related through verbal-noun formation and phonetic shortening.", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q05/p1", "position": "They are equivalent forms for a visitor, apparition or satanic prompting.", "reasons": "Some Basrans compare mayyit/mayt; al-Farra, Ibn Abbas, al-Farisi and others treat the forms as synonymous or dialectal. Ṭāʾif can be a source noun on fāʿil, or a participle from either ṭāfa yaṭūfu or yaṭīfu. Poetic phantoms and jinn visitors are cited by al-Tabari, al-A'sha and Hassan. Al-Akhfash calls ṭayf the more common form. Al-Suhayli denies an active participle for an unreal dream visitor, but allows the real visitor of 68:19; Abu Hayyan also cites that verse."}, {"id": "7:201/q05/p2", "position": "Ṭāʾif circles as an active visitor; ṭayf is a fleeting touch, thought, apparition or madness.", "reasons": "Abu Amr, al-Kisai and others distinguish the circling agent from the touch or whisper. Al-Farisi calls ṭayf a passing thought and ṭāʾif a visitor or thought. Al-Suhayli makes ṭayf an unreal image, ṭāʾif Satan or a real visitor, citing 68:19. Jishumi transmits ṭayf as madness. Ibn Atiyya objects with al-A'sha's jinn visitation; Abu Hayyan and al-Samin defend al-Kisai, arguing a jinn affliction can circle and the poem need not concern a human target."}, {"id": "7:201/q05/p3", "position": "Ṭayf is a verbal noun of ṭāfa yaṭīfu, or a shortened doubled-yāʾ form.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda and al-Tabari cite yaṭīf in poetry. Ibn al-Anbari derives it from ṭayyif, with one yāʾ omitted like hayyin and mayyit; Sa'id's doubled reading supports him. Some derive it from the waw root; Abu al-Baqa proposes changing waw to ya, but al-Samin calls this remote and says the preceding vowel is not kasra. Al-Nahhas answers al-Asma'i's objection to the fīʿl verbal-noun pattern by taking the word as equivalent to ṭāʾif."}]}
{"id": "7:201/q06", "question": "Why depict the temptation as a circling visitor?", "turns_on": "Whether the image stresses harmless superficial contact or the agency of a circling visitor.", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q06/p1", "position": "It suggests a fleeting, slight contact that fails to penetrate the pious.", "reasons": "Baydawi and Alusi liken it to circling without effect; Alusi adds that indefiniteness belittles the touch. Ibn Ashur develops the visiting guest who circles before permission to enter. Biqai adds that Satan sometimes surrounds them or affects them, but his circuit may also pass without effect."}, {"id": "7:201/q06/p2", "position": "It marks an active circling agent, unlike ṭayf's phantom or passing image.", "reasons": "Qiraat-ER contrasts the connotations of the two readings; Ibn Ashur says the familiar dream image is the sense of ṭayf."}]}
{"id": "7:201/q07", "question": "Who or what is 'Satan' here?", "turns_on": "Whether the definite article denotes the devil-kind or Iblis as commander of devils.", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q07/p1", "position": "Satan means devils generically, rather than Iblis alone.", "reasons": "Baydawi and Alusi use the plural pronoun in the next verse as evidence for a collective species."}, {"id": "7:201/q07/p2", "position": "The definite noun may refer to Iblis, whose army whispers by his command.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur gives this alongside the generic possibility."}]}
{"id": "7:201/q08", "question": "How does 'from Satan' attach to the visitation?", "turns_on": "Whether ṭāʾif itself is Satan or his whisper.", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q08/p1", "position": "Min explains the circling visitor if that visitor is Satan himself.", "reasons": "Tabatabai correlates this construction with the interpretation of Satan circling the heart to cast a whisper."}, {"id": "7:201/q08/p2", "position": "Min marks origin if the circling visitor is the whisper sent by Satan.", "reasons": "Tabatabai correlates this construction with a whisper circling until it enters and settles, and says the two interpretations converge."}]}
{"id": "7:201/q09", "question": "How is 'they remembered' read?", "turns_on": "The reported variant wording and the grammatical objection to doubling dhāl.", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q09/p1", "position": "Tadhakkarū, the verse's usual reading.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas says the proposed doubled-dhal form has no grammatical basis."}, {"id": "7:201/q09/p2", "position": "Tadhdhakkarū, with doubled dhāl.", "reasons": "Attributed to Mujahid by al-Nahhas and to Sa'id ibn Jubayr by al-Qurtubi; al-Nahhas objects to its grammar."}, {"id": "7:201/q09/p3", "position": "Taʾammalū, 'they reflected,' replaces tadhakkarū.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi attributes a variant to Ibn al-Zubayr; Ibn Atiyya reports Ibn al-Zubayr's reading and a reordered wording in Ubayy's codex."}]}
{"id": "7:201/q10", "question": "What do the pious remember or do in remembrance?", "turns_on": "What recollection is foregrounded: commands and consequences, reflection on proof, refuge, divine lordship, or God's power and favors.", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q10/p1", "position": "They recall God's commands, prohibitions, reward, punishment, promises and threats.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir name reward and punishment; Razi says blessings and severe punishment turn natural impulse toward divine law. Ibn Atiyya links remembrance to the prior refuge command and to commands and prohibitions; Ibn Ashur calls it bringing prior knowledge to mind and cites 3:135. Alusi also reports Satan's enmity and guile. Biqai includes whatever benefits action and restraint."}, {"id": "7:201/q10/p2", "position": "They reflect on proof, recognize the mistake or danger, and take heed.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Zubayr glosses remembrance as reflection; Zajjaj and Abu Ishaq say they contemplate God's clear proof. Al-Mawardi transmits recognition of danger and a separate account of reflection leading to guidance. Tabatabai says reflection recovers a conclusion previously overlooked or unknown; Study Quran includes 'take heed.'"}, {"id": "7:201/q10/p3", "position": "They seek refuge in God, pray, or rely on Him.", "reasons": "Ataa reports from Ibn Abbas that they seek God's protection then perceive His greatness. Abu Rawq says they supplicate earnestly; Ibn Bahr says remembrance is refuge. Abu al-Suud adds reliance, and Tabatabai explains refuge as recognizing God as sole support. Ibn Ashur includes refuge within the broader practice of remembrance and conjectures this community was especially given refuge, as it was given Friday."}, {"id": "7:201/q10/p4", "position": "They remember God's lordship and oneness, seeing Him as the sole agent.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says they recall God as owner and nurturer, entrust affairs to Him and dispel heedlessness. Qashani and Alusi give the inward account in which attribution to another agent is the touch and recollection of tawhid restores sight."}, {"id": "7:201/q10/p5", "position": "They recall God's power and favors.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas connects this recollection to abandoning the sin and recovering sight; Razi also mentions blessings and punishment."}]}
{"id": "7:201/q11", "question": "What does it mean that they become 'seeing'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q11/p1", "position": "They regain insight into truth, guidance, error and Satan's schemes, then leave the wrong path.", "reasons": "Zajjaj calls it sight with insight. Al-Farra makes it stopping on seeing; al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi make it spotting the error. Ibn Atiyya and al-Tabrisi stress turning to truth and the right path. Baydawi, Bursevi and Alusi add seeing Satan's snares; Tabatabai describes the veil of heedlessness lifting. Islahi and Study Quran emphasize clarified vision and sound judgment."}]}
{"id": "7:201/q12", "question": "Why say mubṣirūn rather than yubsirūn?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q12/p1", "position": "The noun indicates restoration of an enduring quality of insight, immediately and stably.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan and al-Samarrai contrast yubsirun, which would suggest newly acquired seeing. Al-Biqai says the nominal clause and suddenness particle portray immediate stable light of the heart."}]}
{"id": "7:201/q13", "question": "What is the force of the two occurrences of idhā?", "turns_on": "Whether the focus is the two particles' syntax and sudden result or a contrast with in in the preceding verse.", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q13/p1", "position": "The first is temporal and conditional; the second is suddenative, marking immediate insight.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi compares the second with 'I went out, and behold Zayd'; al-Tabrisi and Razi give the same division. Al-Wahidi distinguishes temporal idha from in and cites al-Shafi'i's conditional-divorce example. Ibn Ashur points to the result fa and sudden idha as signs that firm remembrance promptly leads to action."}, {"id": "7:201/q13/p2", "position": "Idhā makes a satanic touch for the pious certain or more likely than the Prophet's possible touch expressed by in.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan contrasts the conditional particles in 7:200 and this verse and explicitly favors this explanation."}]}

{"id": "7:201/q15", "question": "How does this verse relate to the preceding command and following contrast?", "turns_on": "Whether the connection being explained is the refuge command, the forgiveness setting, or the contrast with the next verse.", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q15/p1", "position": "It confirms and explains the prior command to seek refuge from Satan, extending its example to the pious.", "reasons": "Biqai notes the emphatic general statement after the singular prophetic address in 7:200. Alusi says refuge is their settled practice, unlike the astray. Ibn Ashur says in marks importance, and the explanation is broader than the command because remembrance includes more than refuge. Tabatabai parallels 16:99 on Satan's lack of authority over believers who rely on God. Baydawi, Nasafi and others call it confirmation."}, {"id": "7:201/q15/p2", "position": "It helps the Prophet and believers withstand provocation after the command to forgive opponents.", "reasons": "Islahi situates the counsel amid opponents' baseless objections and says the singular command addresses all Muslims. Kuran Yolu ties 7:199 to anger and retaliation, calling for refuge, patience and tolerance."}, {"id": "7:201/q15/p3", "position": "The next verse contrasts the pious with unbelievers extended in error by satanic brothers.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan says the description of the God-fearing ends at 'mubṣirūn'; the subsequent 'yamuddūnahum' refers to Meccan unbelievers."}, {"id": "7:201/q15/p4", "position": "An earlier statement is connected, but the surviving excerpt does not identify it.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi's coherence note is cut off before the earlier statement is named."}]}
{"id": "7:201/q16", "question": "What does the verse imply about prophetic and ordinary vulnerability to Satan?", "turns_on": "Whether the focus is susceptibility, prophetic protection, or the enduring status of a repentant believer.", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q16/p1", "position": "Even the pious may be touched by Satan; prophets alone are infallible.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya argues this from the verse's praise of the pious despite a satanic touch. Razi says the Prophet can receive an initial nudge while the pious may receive a stronger touch; Abu Hayyan contrasts in and idha."}, {"id": "7:201/q16/p2", "position": "The Prophet is specially protected or faces Satan's more intense effort.", "reasons": "Some distinguish the Prophet's initial nazgh from non-prophets' established mass as favor. Another explanation says Satan expends greater effort against the perfect. Ibn Ashur calls the Messenger pious and invites following earlier pious exemplars, citing 6:90."}, {"id": "7:201/q16/p3", "position": "A believer remains God-fearing after a lapse if he repents.", "reasons": "Muhammad ibn Ka'b says God does not call such a person unbeliever; al-Hasan emphasizes nearness through repentance. A Prophetic comparison likens a believer to a stalk that bends and straightens, ending well."}]}
{"id": "7:201/q17", "question": "How can remembering God dissolve anger?", "turns_on": "Whether restraint is explained through a detailed analysis of anger's assumptions or through remembrance of divine anger and refuge.", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q17/p1", "position": "It corrects the judgments that sustain anger and redirects the person toward restraint and forgiveness.", "reasons": "Razi says anger assumes the offender is blameworthy, retaliation possible and the target defenseless. Divine decree and foreknowledge undermine the first; God could punish the angry person, so the last two are false. A report attributed to the Prophet says knowing God's secret in decree eases affliction; Razi gives no grading. He adds that revenge resembles beasts and snakes, forgiveness prophets and saints, and the target might later retaliate; the considerations remove the satanic whisper."}, {"id": "7:201/q17/p2", "position": "Recall God's anger against transgressors and seek refuge, then restrain one's own anger.", "reasons": "The 'people of meanings' counsel recollecting God's anger to avoid a ruinous act. Ibn Atiyya's Prophetic anger report recommends seeking refuge, and Kuran Yolu connects this with patience toward provocation."}]}
{"id": "7:201/q18", "question": "What reports or examples illustrate the verse's response to temptation?", "turns_on": "These are distinct transmitted incidents and images, rather than competing versions of one event.", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q18/p1", "position": "Hasan ibn Ali answered an insulter gently, leading the man to remorse and affection.", "reasons": "Asim ibn al-Mustaliq recounts insulting Hasan, who answered with Quran, offered help, and changed Asim's attitude; al-Qurtubi cites 7:199 and 12:92."}, {"id": "7:201/q18/p2", "position": "A woman with seizures chose patience and Paradise, and the Prophet prayed she would remain covered.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir transmits Abu Hurayra's report; al-Hakim graded it sound on Muslim's criteria while neither collection included it."}, {"id": "7:201/q18/p3", "position": "A young worshipper died after recalling the verse while tempted by adultery and was promised two gardens.", "reasons": "Ibn Asakir's story says Umar prayed at the grave, cited 55:46, and heard the youth answer that God granted the two gardens twice."}, {"id": "7:201/q18/p4", "position": "A saint's vision portrayed remembrance driving a pig-shaped Satan away from the heart.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports a crystal-like human form, a dark mark between the shoulders and a trunk probing the heart. He separately says Satan whispers through a blood-like route, explains prophetic cupping and the seal, and contrasts the Prophet's submitted companion with Adam's."}]}
{"id": "7:201/q19", "question": "How do inward readings apply the verse to thoughts and the heart?", "turns_on": "Whether the inner reading concerns immediate discernment, tawhid, tests for thoughts, or the contrasting condition of false hearts.", "positions": [{"id": "7:201/q19/p1", "position": "A pure heart recognizes satanic thoughts by the light of taqwa and removes them through remembrance.", "reasons": "Sulami describes inner warning and restraint, linking the latter to 79:40. Al-Ta'wilat al-Najmiyya says the heart sees a prompting as a threat to its clarity. Bursevi's teacher says angels continually cast truth into truthful hearts and a satanic touch makes them perceive and erase the intruder; the Merciful shows truth as truth, whereas Satan reverses it."}, {"id": "7:201/q19/p2", "position": "Satanic touch is attributing an act to other than God; recollection of tawhid restores vision of God's agency.", "reasons": "Qashani and Alusi identify this as the inward gloss, with protection from shirk understood at the level of perceived agency."}, {"id": "7:201/q19/p3", "position": "Angelic and satanic thoughts can be distinguished by their effects, though unlawful or doubtful nourishment obscures discernment.", "reasons": "Bursevi says angelic thoughts lead to good, stable, safe outcomes and delight in worship; contrary effects indicate Satan. Sufi masters say unlawful food prevents distinction; some extend this to food of unknown origin. {"id": "7:204/q06", "question": "Why is ٱلْقُرْءَانُ named again instead of using a pronoun?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:204/q06/p1", "position": "The explicit name honors the Qur'an, stresses the instruction, and makes it stand on its own.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls this an eloquent usage; al-Ṭībī says the name brings out why accepting and obeying it produces mercy."}]}
{"id": "7:204/q07", "question": "In which settings does the listening command apply?", "turns_on": "The force of the unrestricted imperative and idhā, the reported occasion, the Meccan context, and the Prophetic and juristic evidence for prayer and sermons.", "positions": [{"id": "7:204/q07/p1", "position": "Obligation is confined to prayer, especially hearing the imam; ordinary recitation outside prayer does not forbid speech.", "reasons": "Mujāhid explicitly permits talk outside prayer; ʿUbayd and ʿAṭāʾ conversed while a storyteller spoke. The sermon occasion is challenged because the verse is Meccan, sermons began after migration, and only brief Qur'an is usually recited there; Ibn al-ʿArabī says silence covers the entire sermon."}, {"id": "7:204/q07/p4", "position": "It governs both prayer and the Friday sermon.", "reasons": "Jābir names these two settings; Ṭabarī invokes a sound imam report, consensus on sermons, and the verse's general wording. ITQAN notes an imperative can signal recommendation or permission."}, {"id": "7:204/q07/p8", "position": "It covers prescribed prayer and gatherings of divine remembrance.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan's reports extend the command beyond the formal prayer to remembrance."}, {"id": "7:204/q07/p9", "position": "The command primarily calls disbelievers to hear the Prophet's Qur'an at the initial proclamation.", "reasons": "Rāzī says this preserves the sequence of demands for signs and the Qur'an's sufficiency, exposes its eloquence and knowledge, and answers 41:26; hoped-for mercy suits unbelievers. {"id": "7:204/q10", "question": "To whom does the pronoun in لَهُۥ refer?", "turns_on": "The nearest named antecedent versus God as the speaker through the revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "7:204/q10/p1", "position": "It refers to the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn connects the phrase to استمعوا, 'for its sake.'"}, {"id": "7:204/q10/p2", "position": "It refers to God, the speaker through the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ permits the pronoun to mean 'for God,' which al-Samīn finds unlikely; Ālūsī gives the inward ground that God speaks through the Qur'an."}]}
{"id": "7:204/q11", "question": "How does the lām in لَهُۥ work?", "turns_on": "Whether the preposition retains purpose, substitutes for ilā, or is syntactically extra.", "positions": [{"id": "7:204/q11/p1", "position": "It indicates purpose: listen for the Qur'an's sake.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn attaches it to استمعوا; Ālūsī includes purpose among the possibilities."}, {"id": "7:204/q11/p2", "position": "It stands for ilā, 'to'.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ and Ālūsī allow this; al-Samīn finds it unnecessary."}, {"id": "7:204/q11/p3", "position": "It is extra, equivalent to 'listen to it' as a direct object.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ permits it, while al-Samīn notes most grammarians allow the extra lām only with an advanced object or a derived governing form; Ālūsī also lists it."}]}

{"id": "7:204/q14", "question": "What must a follower recite while an imam leads prayer?", "turns_on": "Whether silence includes inaudible personal recitation, and how the general command relates to the specific Fātiḥa reports and the report that an imam's reading suffices.", "positions": [{"id": "7:204/q14/p1", "position": "A follower must not recite aloud or answer warning and mercy verses while the imam recites.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd rebukes reciting along, Mujāhid forbids verbal responses to warning or mercy, and the Prophet's report commands following the imam and quiet during his recitation.
